strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper convincingly argues, via a concrete failure-case example (django migration bug), that lack of long-term repository memory limits current code localization agents, drawing a clear analogy to how human developers accumulate codebase knowledge.

The proposed episodic (commit/issue retrieval) and semantic (hotspot file summarization) memory mechanisms are simple, lightweight, and modular, integrating cleanly into an existing SOTA framework (LocAgent) without architectural overhaul.

Consistent and non-trivial empirical gains across two benchmarks (SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live), with careful leakage control (removing issues/commits with overlapping text with test instances).

Thorough ablation studies: episodic-only vs semantic-only vs combined, sensitivity to K in semantic memory construction, and comparison of retrieval methods (BM25 with LLM tokenizer vs standard tokenizer vs dense retrieval), providing useful insights (e.g., sparse retrieval outperforming dense retrieval for code-entity vocabulary).

Goes beyond the localization proxy metric to show downstream impact on end-to-end issue resolution rate using the Agentless patch-generation pipeline, strengthening the practical significance of the results.

Insightful behavioral and efficiency analysis (tool-use shift toward hypothesis-driven investigation, per-example cost variance, correlation between commit-history richness and performance gains) that adds depth beyond aggregate accuracy numbers.
Honest reporting of limitations, including performance degradation in repositories with sparse commit history and acknowledgment of noisy issue-commit linking, which strengthens credibility.
Good reproducibility: detailed tool documentation, example agent trajectories, and prompts provided in appendices.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies on a single, somewhat dated backbone (GPT-4o, 2024-05-13); no experiments demonstrating the approach generalizes across different LLM backbones or model scales, which limits confidence in the generality of the reported gains.

Despite claiming the memory tools are 'modular' and 'easily integrated into existing agentic frameworks,' the paper only demonstrates integration with LocAgent; no actual experiments integrate the memory mechanisms into other frameworks (e.g., Agentless, SWE-agent) to substantiate this generality claim.

The SWE-bench-live evaluation subset is small and pre-filtered (130 examples, instances requiring ≤5 file edits), which may inflate performance and limits how representative the results are of the full, more diverse benchmark.

The technical contribution is somewhat incremental: BM25-based commit retrieval and LLM-generated file summaries are standard techniques: the core novelty lies mainly in the application/framing (repository memory for localization) rather than in new methodology.

No direct comparison against other memory-augmented or experience-driven agent baselines (e.g., the cited SWE-exp) applied to the same localization task, making it hard to contextualize how much of the gain is specific to this design versus general benefit of any memory mechanism.

Semantic memory construction uses a fixed, simplistic 'most frequently edited files' heuristic tuned primarily on a single repository (Django) and then applied uniformly across all repos, despite the paper itself acknowledging more principled JiT-SDP-inspired strategies could improve results.

Performance clearly degrades on repositories with limited commit history (Table 2, 'others' group -13.1), and the paper does not propose or test any mechanism (beyond future-work discussion) to mitigate this failure mode, meaning the method's benefit is conditional and somewhat narrow in scope.
Results appear to be based on single runs without reported variance/statistical significance testing, which is a common concern for agentic benchmark evaluations where trajectories can be stochastic.

strengths: Well-motivated and intuitive idea: using repository commit history as a non-parametric memory source (episodic + semantic) to augment code localization agents, addressing a genuine limitation of prior 'memoryless' agentic approaches.

The proposed memory tools (SearchCommit, ExamineCommit, ViewSummary, SearchSummary) are simple, modular, and easily integrated into an existing SOTA framework (LocAgent) without architectural changes.

Solid empirical evaluation on two benchmarks (SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live) with consistent improvements over strong baselines (LocAgent, Agentless, CodeRankEmbed), and useful ablations isolating the contribution of episodic vs. semantic memory.

Rich supplementary analyses: per-repository breakdown correlating gains with commit history richness, tool-use distribution shift analysis showing a behavioral change toward hypothesis-driven search, cost/efficiency analysis at the instance level, and a comparison of sparse vs. dense retrieval for memory interfaces.
Reasonably transparent error analysis and discussion of limitations (e.g., performance degradation on repos with sparse commit history), which strengthens the credibility of the claims.
Care taken to prevent data leakage (filtering commits/issues with overlapping text with test instances, restricting to commits prior to issue base commit).
weaknesses: Missing direct empirical comparison to the most closely related prior work (Chen et al. 2025a, SWE-exp) on memory-augmented agents, despite explicitly citing it as 'the most related work'; this weakens the positioning and novelty claims.

Evaluation is restricted to a single backbone LLM (GPT-4o, 2024-05-13), leaving open whether gains generalize to other/newer models, and the SWE-bench-live evaluation subset is quite small (130 examples across 62 repos), limiting statistical robustness.

The paper only evaluates the localization sub-task and does not report end-to-end SWE-bench resolution rates (patch generation/test pass), so the practical downstream impact of improved localization remains unverified.

No comparison against simpler non-agentic baselines that could exploit commit history similarly (e.g., directly prepending relevant commit summaries to a procedural/Agentless-style prompt), which would help isolate whether the benefit comes from the memory content itself or from the agentic tool-based retrieval mechanism.

The method's benefit is highly repository-dependent and can hurt performance (-13.1 Acc@5 on 'others' group with sparse commit history), and no concrete mitigation (e.g., a mechanism to decide when to trust memory) is implemented, only proposed as future work.

Preprocessing/construction costs of the memory (e.g., LLM-generated summaries for 200 files per repo, embedding/searching thousands of commits) are not quantified, leaving practical scalability and overhead unclear.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental, combining largely standard techniques (BM25 retrieval, LLM-based summarization) rather than introducing a fundamentally new memory mechanism or learning-based component.

Absolute performance gains, while consistent, are moderate (roughly 3-5 points Acc@5), and cost increases are non-trivial even on already-correctly-solved instances, raising questions about overall cost-effectiveness in practice.
